source_text: Per quid igitur sub diabolo sunt, quos Deus fecit? Per peccatum non per naturam Sed ut non potest sine sexibus esse fetus, ita nec sine voluntate delictum Dicis enim ideo illos esse sub diabolo, quia de sexus utriusque commixtione nascuntur
pass_a_gloss: Through what therefore are they under the devil, whom God made? Through sin, not through nature. But as there cannot be offspring without the sexes, so neither a crime without the will. For you say they are under the devil because they are born from the mixing of each sex.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: Through what, then, are those whom God made under the devil?
But just as there can be no offspring without the sexes, there can be no sin without the will.
For you say that they are under the devil because they are born from the union of the two sexes.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, De nuptiis et concupiscentia 2 / On Marriage and Concupiscence); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
kind: Julian excerpt in the intermediary document
